newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian govt orders police probe of key senator.
newsitem.headline: Australian govt orders police probe of key senator.

text.p: Australia's conservative government, embroiled in a deepening scandal over abuse of perks, on Tuesday demanded a key independent senator stand aside while police investigate claims of dishonesty against him.
Prime Minister John Howard, under increasing fire over parliamentary standards in his year-old conservative government, urged Senator Mal Colston stand down as Senate deputy president.
Colston, an independent, is considered crucial for government to pass reforms through a hostile upper house.

"Senator Colston should stand down as deputy president of the Senate and all of the matters in dispute relating to his travelling allowance should be referred to the (Australian) Federal Police," Howard told reporters.
Leftist opposition parties and community groups have demanded Colston quit his powerful deputy presidency over allegations he has abused parliamentary benefits.

Colston, a Labor opposition defector now sitting as an independent in the upper house Senate, has been accused of claiming travel allowances when he was at home, misusing his postal allowance and abusing other parliamentary perks.
Until now, Howard had defended Colston as innocent until proven guilty over the charges, the latest to rock his conservative administration.
Earlier on Tuesday, Attorney-General Darly Williams said a government parliamentarian and a recently retired colleague would be charged with fraud over travel and car claims.
Lower house National Party MP Michael Cobb and former Liberal senator Bob Woods, who both deny any wrongdoing, will face court after police investigated claims of expenses abuse, Williams said.

Howard, who led the conservative Liberal-National alliance to power a year ago after 13 years in opposition, has pledged to lift parliamentary standards and restore public confidence in politicians. He also has implemented a new code of conduct.
Colston repaid A$6,880 (US$5,300) last month after a Senate inquiry found he had wrongly claimed 43 days of travel allowances in less than four years. He blamed a book-keeping error by an employee.
That staff member Christine Smith took responsibility for the error, saying she had kept poor records and prepared incorrect claims but on Tuesday she recanted.

Opposition Senate Leader John Faulkner on Tuesday produced a letter in which Smith said: "I was not responsible for preparing the senator's travelling allowance claims nor required to keep a record of dates of travel for (travelling allowance) purposes.
"The senator always prepared his own claims."

The national police union on Tuesday had demanded Howard launch an official probe into allegations against Colston, saying the high-profile affair had become politicised and only an independent probe could clear the air.
"Nobody knows what to believe as a result of this contrived environment of media frenzy and political point-scoring," said police union chief Chris Eaton.

Labor, which has vowed revenge on Colston for "ratting" on the party, has accused Howard of buying his support with the deputy presidency and extra perks for his staff. Howard and Colston dismiss the charges as spiteful.

If Colston were convicted of fraud, he could no longer sit in the Senate. That would throw the fate of future government legislation, including its 1997/98 budget, into doubt because he would be replaced by a Labor member since he was elected as a Labor member.
